### The Dusty Dinosaurs off Route 12

Long before *Jurassic Park*, the Prehistoric Forest was a roadside attraction that operated from 1963 to 1999. This dinosaur theme park was located in the Irish Hills of Michigan, just off U.S. Route 12, and was designed to attract Detroiters vacationing at nearby lakes. Today, visitors can still see the ruins of this once-popular park.

The Prehistoric Forest offered a campy charm with over 70 fiberglass statues of dinosaurs and other extinct creatures, including a woolly mammoth, Neanderthals, and pterodactyls. Its centerpiece was a giant fiberglass volcano featuring a working waterfall. Visitors could ride a train around the park while a safari guide pointed out the dinosaurs, providing educational insights about when they lived, what they ate, and when they disappeared.

The dinosaurs, reminiscent of the stop-motion creatures from *King Kong* (1933) and *The Lost World* (1925), were created by James Q. Sidwell, a dinosaur expert who had previously worked at the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago. Sidwell also designed creatures for Dinosaur Land in Virginia and the Prehistoric Forest in Marblehead, Ohio, a park featured in the film *Tommy Boy*, which closed in 2010.

The tourist traps along Route 12 began to decline following the completion of the Michigan leg of Interstate 94 in 1972. This led to a significant drop in visitors, causing many local businesses to suffer. In the final years of its operation, the Prehistoric Forest faced frequent vandalism. In 2010, high school students stole several statues and placed them on the school's roof. Two years later, another group broke in at night, beheading and dismembering most remaining statues.

After closure, the park fell into disrepair, with nature reclaiming the area around the dinosaurs, which began to look lifelike as the forest grew wild around them. The volcano eventually crumbled, resembling a crater. Vandals left messages on its base, including one that read, "I remember coming here as a kid. I wanted to be a dinosaur."

In 2019, the park was purchased by the owner of a local petroleum company, who initially believed the dinosaurs could be standing atop an oil deposit. However, after seeing the decaying statues, she fell in love with them and decided to save the park. As of now, no renovations have taken place, and the dinosaurs remain, mere shadows of their former selves.

The story of the Prehistoric Forest holds personal significance for me. On Holy Saturday, in the drizzling rain, I visited the park with my girlfriend. Beneath the jaws of the T. Rex, I proposed to her, and much like the dinosaurs, the memory will last forever.
